title: Account ‘88888’: Cut Out of the Daily Reports in July 1992, £830 Million by 27 February 1995
participants: Nick Leeson (General Manager and Head Trader, BFS)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was reputational before it was financial, and it was paid out in bonuses and standing. The Board records that through the whole period Leeson "represented that he was in fact making profits. Indeed, he was perceived within Barings to be a ‘star performer’", while Barings in London understood the profits to come from inter-exchange arbitrage — "switching" between SIMEX and the Japanese exchanges — in what it believed were fully matched trades at no real risk.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was a line of code, dated. Account ‘88888’ was set up in July 1992 and at inception appeared in four reports sent electronically to London each day: the trade file, the price file, the margin file and London gross. A systems consultant to BFS told the Board that on or around 8 July 1992 he received specific instructions from Leeson to change the software so that account ‘88888’ was excluded from all of them except the margin file, and that this held until the collapse. The Board’s inference is on the record: the exclusion "was designed to exclude the account from the books and records of Barings".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: For two and a half years the account existed and was not seen. London management said "that at no time until Thursday 23 February 1995 were they aware of the existence of account ‘88888’" — although the one report it was never removed from, the margin file, did carry it, "but we were told that this was not noticed or appreciated". The concealment ran on falsified reports to London, misrepresented profitability, and false trading transactions and accounting entries. The exchange itself raised the account by name on 11 January 1995, when SIMEX wrote asking about margin funding that looked like BFS financing customers’ margins to the extent of US$100 million, a figure computed purely by reference to account ‘88888’.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall; there was a funding line that kept paying. The Board found the unauthorised trading was funded by money advanced to BFS by group companies for what they understood to be their own account trading, and by money advanced on BFS’s requests for margin payments to the exchanges — "requests which were met without any effective query and without any adequate steps being taken by Barings in London to verify them or to reconcile the advances to the trading records of clients" — and, in January and February 1995, by artificial trades created to reduce SIMEX margin calls. Losses on the account reached some £208 million by 31 December 1994 and some £830 million by 27 February 1995.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The inquiry that followed states its own limits in the text, which is why it is worth citing. Commenced on 2 March 1995 at the Chancellor’s instigation, reported to him on 13 July and published by order of the House of Commons on 18 July, it concluded that the losses came from unauthorised and concealed trading, that the true position went unnoticed through "a serious failure of controls and managerial confusion within Barings", and that neither the external auditors nor the supervisors nor the regulators had detected it. It recorded that Peter Baring described the failure of controls over BFS as "absolute", and added: "We agree." And it recorded that it had very limited access to documents in Singapore, could not formally interview BFS management or staff or its auditors, and that Leeson gave it nothing. The lessons it drew for the Bank of England were procedural — consolidated supervision, memoranda of understanding with other regulators, an independent quality assurance review of the Bank’s own supervision.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A merchant bank restructuring its banking and securities businesses under one roof from 1992, with group funding available to a Singapore subsidiary on request, and a supervisory regime that looked at the authorised bank rather than at the group around it.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Barings supervisory settlement: consolidated supervision extended to understand risks across a group containing an authorised bank, memoranda of understanding between regulators at home and abroad, and independent quality assurance of the supervisor itself.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The reported profits justified the funding, and the funding financed the losses that the reports concealed. Each margin call answered without query produced a larger position, which produced a larger margin call; the only report that still carried the account was the one nobody read.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That a 28-year-old rogue trader in Singapore brought down a 233-year-old bank on his own, and that nobody at Barings could possibly have known.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The inquiry found the first half and refused the second. Its conclusions are three, in order: the losses came from unauthorised and concealed trading within BFS; the true position went unnoticed "by reason of a serious failure of controls and managerial confusion within Barings"; and it had not been detected before the collapse by the external auditors, the supervisors or the regulators. The Chairman of Barings plc called the failure of controls over BFS "absolute", and the Board agreed. The account the bank supposedly could not see was named in a letter from the exchange six weeks before the collapse and sat in the one daily file it was never cut from. Equally, the inquiry’s own caveat runs against treating it as the last word on Leeson himself: it had very limited access to documents in Singapore, could not interview BFS’s management, staff or auditors, and Leeson "has not provided any information to this inquiry or given his own explanation of events".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Account ‘88888’ was set up in July 1992 and excluded from every daily report to London except the margin file on instructions given on or around 8 July 1992. It carried unauthorised positions for over two and a half years. Accumulated losses on it reached some £208 million by 31 December 1994 and some £830 million by 27 February 1995. It was funded by intra-group advances and unqueried margin requests, and latterly by artificial trades created to reduce SIMEX margin calls. SIMEX raised it by name on 11 January 1995 over US$100 million of apparently mis-funded margin. London says it learned of the account on 23 February 1995; the bank collapsed on 26 February 1995. The Board of Banking Supervision reported to the Chancellor on 13 July 1995 and Parliament published the report on 18 July. Leeson pleaded guilty in a Singapore court on 1 December 1995 to two offences of deceiving the auditors of Barings and cheating SIMEX, and was sentenced to six and a half years’ imprisonment.

citations.title: Report of the Board of Banking Supervision Inquiry into the Circumstances of the Collapse of Barings, HC 673, ordered by the House of Commons to be printed 18 July 1995 (London: HMSO)
citations.quoteOrFact: A 354-page scan with no text layer, served from the UK government's own asset store; downloaded and read page by page in a browser (title page, covering letter, and report pages 3, 78 and 232–233). The covering letter, dated 13 July 1995 on Board of Banking Supervision paper at the Bank of England, is signed by E A J George as Chairman of the Board and Sir Alan Hardcastle as Convenor of the Independent Members. On the concealment, at report page 78, section 5 opens: "The analysis in Section 4 shows that the London client account '88888' maintained within BFS had been used by Leeson for over two and a half years to take unauthorised trading positions. The fact that Leeson was able to conceal the positions and losses recorded in this account caused the collapse of Barings on 26 February 1995." The report records that account '88888' "was set up in July 1992", that it was at inception included in four daily electronic reports to London, and that a systems consultant to BFS, Dr Edmund Wong, informed the Board that he had received "on or around 8 July 1992, specific instructions from Leeson to change the software program to exclude account '88888' from all these reports, with the exception of the margin file", and that this "continued to be the case throughout the period up to the collapse on 26 February 1995"; the Board's inference is stated: "It appears, therefore, that Leeson intended to use account '88888' for unauthorised activity from the outset, and that the action noted above was designed to exclude the account from the books and records of Barings." It records that "In London, Barings' management and other personnel have said that at no time until Thursday 23 February 1995 were they aware of the existence of account '88888'", though the margin file sent to London did include it "but we were told that this was not noticed or appreciated". It also records that SIMEX wrote to Jones on 11 January 1995 expressing concern about the funding of margin in respect of the "BSL - Customer Segregated Account" and suggesting "it appeared that BFS might be financing the margins of customers - which is against the rules of SIMEX - to the extent of US$100 million", an amount "computed purely by reference to account '88888'". Section 13, at report page 232, states the conclusions: "(a) the losses were incurred by reason of unauthorised and concealed trading activities within BFS; (b) the true position was not noticed earlier by reason of a serious failure of controls and managerial confusion within Barings; and (c) the true position had not been detected prior to the collapse by the external auditors, supervisors or regulators of Barings." The scale is given in the same section: losses on account '88888' of "some £208 million" by 31 December 1994 and "some £830 million" by 27 February 1995, accumulated while "he represented that he was in fact making profits. Indeed, he was perceived within Barings to be a 'star performer'." Paragraph 13.8 lists the devices: "the suppression of account '88888' from Barings in London (which account was mentioned only in the margin files and did not attract the attention of Barings in London); the submission of falsified reports to London; the misrepresentation of the profitability of BFS's trading; and a number of false trading transactions and accounting entries." Paragraph 13.10 records that the Chairman of Barings plc, Peter Baring, "described the failure of controls with regard to BFS as 'absolute'. We agree." THE BOARD'S OWN CAVEAT, at paragraph 13.1, is part of the record and is reproduced here: "we have had very limited access to documents of BFS or SIMEX in Singapore and we have not been able to conduct formal interviews with the senior management, or more junior staff, of BFS in Singapore. Nor have we been able to see the work papers of, or interview, BFS's auditors. Further, Leeson, the General Manager and Head Trader of BFS — who, from any viewpoint, is a central figure in the events leading to the collapse of Barings — has not provided any information to this inquiry or given his own explanation of events."

citations.title: Bank of England, Banking Act Report 1995/96 — Report of the Board of Banking Supervision, "Inquiry into the Collapse of Barings"
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Bank of England's own archive and read as extracted text; the file is an OCR'd scan whose text layer is imperfect, so it is used here for dates, sequence and the Board's own summary rather than for fine wording. The Board's annual report records that the inquiry began on 2 March 1995 "at the instigation of the Chancellor of the Exchequer", with the aims of establishing in detail the events that led to the collapse, reaching immediately applicable conclusions, and identifying the lessons for institutions, for the Bank's own regulatory and supervisory arrangements and for the UK system of regulation generally. It records that the Board's report "was provided to the Chancellor on 13 July 1995 and published by order of the House of Commons on 18 July", and restates the same three summary conclusions carried in section 13 of the report itself. It confirms the Board's own limits: "The Board was unable to get full access to information in Singapore or to conduct formal interviews with BFS's management, employees and staff or to interview BFS's auditors", and that the inquiry was not able to speak to Mr Nick Leeson, formerly General Manager and Head Trader of Baring Futures (Singapore). On what followed: in September 1995, after publication, "a report was published by inspectors appointed by the Singaporean Minister of Finance to investigate the affairs of BFS" — that report was not read here — and "On 1 December, Mr Leeson pleaded guilty in a Singapore court to two offences of deceiving the auditors of Barings and to cheating the Singapore International Monetary Exchange. He was sentenced to six and a half years' imprisonment." The Bank's own follow-through is recorded in the same report: the key recommendations for the Bank were extending consolidated supervision, developing regulatory co-operation through Memoranda of Understanding with other regulators in the UK and overseas, and the introduction of an independent quality assurance review of the Bank's supervision of banks.
